newsitem.title: SPAIN: Telefonica chief hawks shares as sale launched.
newsitem.headline: Telefonica chief hawks shares as sale launched.

text.p: Spain's Telefonica de Espana has turned to chairman Juan Villalonga for a media blitz to promote the launch on Monday of the privatisation of the state's remaining 20.9 percent stake.
Villalonga took advantage of the weekend to assure potential buyers through various media that the sale, whose subscription period begins today, will be a success.
The placement -- the largest in Spain's history -- is focused on retail customers. Villalonga would like the ranks of individual investors in the telecoms operator to swell by 200,000 to one million.
"The goal for the sale is to reach one million individual shareholders by the end of the operation," Villalonga said in an interview published on Monday in the financial daily Gaceta de los Negocios.
"For those Spaniards who want to invest, Telefonica is the safest and most profitable share on the Spanish bourse."
Speaking to daily La Vanguardia, he dismissed criticism that Telefonica's share price had risen too much.
"For new investors, what is important is not today's price, but the price in the future," he said.
Telefonica's share price doubled in the last 12 months to close Friday at 3,340 pesetas. On Monday, it gained more than two percent to reach a new peak of 3,420 pesetas in early trade.
Villalonga said he was not concerned by the competition the company would face with the full liberalisation of the sector by November 1998.
"We are convinced that the loss of market share will be compensated many times over by market growth," he told the daily El Mundo.
Currently, Telefonica enjoys a monopoly on basic telephone services, because the second operator, Retevision, still hasn't begun to offer its services.

Analysts expect its market share to fall by between 15 and 25 percent by the year 2000. In mobile telephones, Airtel has fought Telefonica aggressively for new clients. Airtel now has 650,000 clients compared to Telefonica's 1.7 million.
The competition will not only raise the battle for clients, but should also press prices lower, particularly in long-distance fares.
But Villalonga expects to neutralise this effect. In the next four years, the groups wants to have one out of every two pesetas of its earnings from its international business.
Telefonica has operations in Chile, Argentina, Venezuela, Brazil and Peru through its subsidiary Telefonica Internacional TISA.
